marks.gloss: value as what holds rather than what is: binding whether or not anyone wants, knows or does it — truth holding of a theorem, justice holding of a case no court has heard
marks.source: Lotze, Logik §§316–318; Rickert, Der Gegenstand der Erkenntnis

marks.gloss: value's negative pole, which is not its absence: the false, the ugly, the unjust, holding as what ought not to be — an error, a cruelty, a botched work
marks.source: Rickert, value and counter-value (Wert und Unwert)

marks.gloss: value as it faces someone who can fail it: a demand, a norm — 'judge truly', 'keep the promise'; unlike a law of nature it can be broken
marks.source: Windelband, 'Normen und Naturgesetze'; Rickert, the transcendent ought

marks.gloss: a subject's yes or no to an ought: affirming in judgment, approving a deed, honouring a right — or refusing; a real act at a time, by someone
marks.source: Windelband, every judgment contains an appraisal; Rickert, Stellungnahme (taking a position toward a value)

marks.gloss: value as what someone desires or likes: wanting bread, enjoying a song, preferring one coat to another — whether or not anything demands it
marks.source: Lotze (values given in feeling); the psychological value theory of Meinong and Ehrenfels, which the Baden school opposed; Simmel ch. 1 (value and desire)

marks.gloss: a real thing that bears a value: a work, a law, an institution, a theory, a tool well made — value realized in culture
marks.source: Rickert, Kulturwissenschaft und Naturwissenschaft (goods, Güter)

marks.gloss: a reality's mattering for a value, apart from whether anyone approves it: a revolution, a war, a forgery is significant for the values it touches
marks.source: Rickert, value-relation (Wertbeziehung) as distinct from evaluation

marks.gloss: value for the sake of another, relative to need or taste and exchangeable for an equivalent: a market price, a fee, what one would give for it
marks.source: Kant, Groundwork 4:434; Simmel, Philosophie des Geldes ch. 1

axioms: A value holds; it does not exist. Whatever exists — an act, a thing, a price — is real and passes; whatever holds does not pass.
Every value has two poles; the negative pole is not the absence of value but its counter-value.
Where an ought holds, failing it is possible; where failing is impossible there is a law of nature, not an ought.
Whatever has a price can be replaced by an equivalent; what holds has none.
cast.subject: Value as the Neo-Kantians take it, Kant behind them and Simmel beside them: what holds rather than what is, how it faces a subject who can fail it, how it is answered with a yes or a no, borne by real goods, made significant in history, and priced in exchange — read from Lotze, Logik (1874) §§316–318; Windelband, 'Normen und Naturgesetze' (1882, in Präludien); Rickert, Der Gegenstand der Erkenntnis (1892/1904) and Kulturwissenschaft und Naturwissenschaft (1899); Kant, Groundwork 4:434; Simmel, Philosophie des Geldes (1900) ch. 1

file.concept: Value (working name; the corner's name is Arman's to type)
file.cast_by: Virgin Land, 2026-10-09, at Arman's word ('cast our original four concepts in that new shape; drop the logical square; adhere to the concept itself'); poured under MOLD v5 with its amendment §8 of 2026-10-09 (a role is a moment). Every label, word and quality is a proposal until Arman ratifies it.
premises: The Neo-Kantian backbone is Arman's choice of 2026-09-25 ('for value, use neo-kantians'). The logical square of that day (self-value, self-disvalue, conditional value, conditional disvalue) is dropped at his word of 2026-10-09.

Moments are cut by how value shows up and how it moves: it holds; facing a subject it becomes an ought; the subject answers it; the answer, carried into work, becomes a good; the good, once real, matters in history; offered in exchange, it takes a price.

The acknowledging and the wanting are kept as two moments: answering an ought and desiring a thing are two ways value shows up, and the Neo-Kantians' case against psychologism rests on keeping them apart.

Polarity (true and false, beautiful and ugly, just and unjust) is kept as one moment, the counter-value, opposed to the validity, rather than as an axis crossing every moment; it is the negative pole, not the absence of value.
Kant and Simmel are admitted for the price because the Neo-Kantians' own contrast of what holds with what is merely wanted or exchanged needs that moment on the page.
The value-free, mere nature, is left out as the concept's edge; Rickert's third realm of meaning is left out (did_not_fit).
open_forks: Is the significance real? It sits on real things but is a relation to a value; 'exists in time' is written UNKNOWN.
Does the counter-value hold in the same sense as the value? Rickert pairs them; whether 'the false holds' as truth holds is left open.
Does the ought exist in time? Rickert's transcendent ought does not; a promise made today creates an ought that did not exist yesterday. Written 'no', with Rickert.
did_not_fit: Rickert's third realm, meaning (Sinn), the immanent sense of the valuing act (System der Philosophie, 1921): a moment of value in his late system, left out so that Value is not cast toward Meaning.
The ranking of values (higher and lower; Rickert's six domains, 'Vom System der Werte', 1913): an ordering among values, not a moment of value; the mold forbids handing in a ranking.
The value-free, nature as mere reality: the concept's edge.

derived_check.ordering: passes into, read as directed: validity → ought → acknowledging → good → significance; good → price; wanting → price. Refused: validity ↛ price, price ↛ validity, significance ↛ validity. Two roots, what holds and what is wanted, meeting only in the good's price; no movement returns to the validity. Marked derived.

passes into.meaning: the first, carried through, becomes the second: the concept's own movement from one moment to the next

presupposes.meaning: the first cannot be what it is unless the second is given

is borne by.meaning: the first is present in the second as in its bearer

opposes.meaning: the first and the second are the two poles of one value, each excluding the other

0.reason: a value that holds, faced by a subject who can fall short of it, becomes a demand: truth turns into the ought of judging truly (Rickert, the transcendent ought; Windelband, 'Normen und Naturgesetze')

1.reason: a demand is met by a yes or a no: to judge is to affirm what ought to be affirmed (Windelband; Rickert, Der Gegenstand der Erkenntnis)

2.reason: a value affirmed and carried into work becomes a good: the affirmed truth a theory, the honoured right a law (Rickert, Kulturwissenschaft und Naturwissenschaft)

3.reason: a good, once real, comes to matter beyond its makers' approval: it becomes significant for whoever relates it to its value (Rickert, value-relation)

4.reason: a good offered in exchange takes on a price: its value becomes what another would give for it (Simmel, Philosophie des Geldes ch. 1)

5.reason: what holds has no equivalent: it is raised above all price (Kant, Groundwork 4:434)

6.reason: no price, however high, makes a thing hold: whatever has a price can be replaced by an equivalent (Kant, Groundwork 4:434)

7.reason: no amount of mattering in history makes a value hold: validity is not made by significance (Windelband's and Rickert's case against historicism)

8.reason: there is no ought without a value that holds: a norm is a value turned toward a subject (Windelband)

9.reason: an ought addresses only one who could fail it; where failing were impossible there would be a law of nature, not a norm (Windelband, 'Normen und Naturgesetze')

10.reason: a truth holds whether or not anyone affirms it (Lotze, Logik §316; Rickert against psychologism)

11.reason: a price exists only where someone wants: market price is relative to need, fancy price to taste (Kant, Groundwork 4:434)

12.reason: a reality matters only relative to a value that holds (Rickert: value-relation presupposes values)

13.reason: a thing can matter for a value without anyone approving it: the historian relates a war to political values without praising it (Rickert, Kulturwissenschaft und Naturwissenschaft: value-relation is not evaluation)

14.reason: a value that holds is present in a good as in its bearer: justice in a law, truth in a theory (Rickert: goods are realities to which values attach)

15.reason: a value is not in the act that affirms it: the act is real and passes, the value holds (Rickert against psychologism)

16.reason: a price sits on a thing offered in exchange (Simmel ch. 1)

17.reason: true and false, beautiful and ugly, just and unjust: the two poles of one value, each excluding the other (Rickert, Wert und Unwert)

18.reason: the same opposition read from the negative pole; listed both ways because the word is symmetric

19.reason: what holds does not hold because it is wanted: value is not desirability (the Baden school against the psychological value theory of Meinong and Ehrenfels)

20.reason: a yes or no is an acknowledging only as the answer to a demand; a mere liking is wanting, not acknowledging (Rickert)

21.reason: one can want what no ought demands, and want what an ought forbids

22.reason: a want that meets a thing another holds becomes an offer: desire, through exchange, sets a price (Simmel, Philosophie des Geldes ch. 1)

marks.gloss: a way things could stand, before or apart from whether it does: the cat's being on the mat, the train's arriving at nine
marks.source: Tractatus 2.012–2.0141 (states of affairs and their possibility)

marks.gloss: a way things stand: what is the case, here and now — the cat is on the mat
marks.source: Tractatus 2: what is the case, a fact, is the existence of states of affairs

marks.gloss: a way things could stand that does not, which is itself the case: there is no cat on the mat; the train did not come
marks.source: Tractatus 2.06; Russell, Logical Atomism III (negative facts)

marks.gloss: that these are all the facts and nothing besides: the world as everything that is the case — 'and that's all'
marks.source: Tractatus 1.1–1.12; Russell, Logical Atomism V (general facts)

marks.gloss: what has been the case and can no longer be otherwise: the battle was fought, the word was said
marks.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.2, 1139b7–11 (citing Agathon)

marks.gloss: a fact ascertained and held so that it can be cited: the facts of the case, a measured value, a date fixed by documents
marks.source: Fleck, Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact; Austin, 'Truth'

marks.gloss: a fact that is the case because it is counted as the case: a debt, a marriage, a border, a goal scored
marks.source: Searle, Construction of Social Reality ch. 2 ('X counts as Y in C'); Anscombe, 'On Brute Facts'

axioms: Every fact is a way things could stand that stands; every negative fact a way things could stand that does not.
What has been the case cannot be made not to have been.
No set of positive facts settles the negative ones without the fact that they are all.
An established fact can be revised; a done fact cannot.
A fact that is the case because it is counted stops being the case when the counting stops.
cast.subject: Fact: what is the case, read as the concept moves — from a way things could stand, to its standing or not standing, to its having been and being settled, to its being ascertained and held, with the totality that settles what is not, and facts that are the case because they are counted — read from Wittgenstein, Tractatus 1–2.06; Russell, The Philosophy of Logical Atomism (1918) lectures III and V; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.2; Austin, 'Truth' (1950); Anscombe, 'On Brute Facts' (1958); Searle, The Construction of Social Reality (1995) ch. 2; Fleck, Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact (1935)

file.concept: Fact (working name; the corner's name is Arman's to type)
file.cast_by: Virgin Land, 2026-10-09, at Arman's word ('cast our original four concepts in that new shape; drop the logical square; adhere to the concept itself'); poured under MOLD v5 with its amendment §8 of 2026-10-09 (a role is a moment). Every label, word and quality is a proposal until Arman ratifies it.
premises: The logical square of 2026-09-25 (general and particular, positive and negative facts) is dropped at Arman's word of 2026-10-09. Two of its insights survive as moments: the not-obtaining (Russell's negative fact) and the totality (Russell's general fact, Wittgenstein's 'all the facts').

Moments are cut by how fact shows up and how it moves: a way things could stand comes to stand or fails to; what stands passes and becomes what has been, which can no longer be otherwise; what has been is ascertained and held; some facts are the case only because they are counted as the case.

Brute facts are the default here; the instituted is the moment where being counted makes a fact the case (Searle), resting on facts that are the case without being counted (Anscombe: bruteness is relative).
The fact as a true thought (Frege) and as what a true statement states (Strawson) are theories of where facts live, not moments of fact (did_not_fit).
open_forks: Does the established pass into the instituted? Fleck and those after him would say a scientific fact is made by its collective; written does-not-hold, with that fork open.
Is the totality a fact among facts (Russell's general fact) or the frame of all facts (Tractatus 1.11)? Kept as one moment.
Are there negative facts, or only the non-existence of positive ones? Kept as a moment because the concept, as used, has them: 'the train did not come' is a fact one reports.
The done: does it pass into the established always, or only when someone takes it up? Most of what has been is never ascertained; the movement is written as the concept's, not as what always happens.
did_not_fit: The fact as a true thought (Frege, 'Der Gedanke', 1918) and as what a true statement states (Strawson, 'Truth', 1950): theories of where facts live, not moments of fact.
The value-laden fact (thick concepts; the entanglement of fact and value): the meeting of Fact with Value is the edge's business, not this cast's.

derived_check.ordering: passes into, read as directed: possible → obtaining → done → established; possible → not-obtaining. Refused: done ↛ obtaining, established ↛ instituted. A line with one branch and no return: the concept runs one way, from could-be to settled and held. Marked derived.

passes into.meaning: the first, carried through, becomes the second: the concept's own movement from one moment to the next

presupposes.meaning: the first cannot be what it is unless the second is given

settles.meaning: the first fixes which instances of the second there are

excludes.meaning: the first and the second cannot both hold of the same way things could stand

0.reason: a way things could stand comes to stand: the coin lands heads (Tractatus 2)

1.reason: a way things could stand fails to stand, and its failing is itself a fact (Tractatus 2.06; Russell, Logical Atomism III)

2.reason: what is the case passes and becomes what has been the case

3.reason: what has been cannot come to be the case again as the same fact; a repetition is another fact (Aristotle, NE VI.2: not even a god can make undone what has been done)

4.reason: what has been the case is taken up, ascertained and recorded, and becomes a fact one can cite (Fleck)

5.reason: ascertaining finds a fact, it does not make one: a fact recorded does not become a fact that is the case by being counted (Searle's line between brute and institutional facts; Fleck would contest it, see open_forks)

6.reason: what is the case is one of the ways things could stand (Tractatus 2.012–2.0141)

7.reason: only what could be the case can fail to be the case: there is no negative fact of the impossible

8.reason: a way things could stand needs nothing to be the case to be possible

9.reason: only what is or was the case can be established; a record of what is not the case is an error, not an established fact

10.reason: what is the case does not wait to be ascertained: the fact comes before its record (Austin, 'Truth': statements correspond to facts, they do not make them)

11.reason: a fact that is the case by being counted needs something that is the case to be counted as it: the paper for money, the words said for a marriage (Searle ch. 2; Anscombe: bruteness is relative)

12.reason: a debt, a border, a price is the case only while it is held as the case and can be cited (Searle: collective acceptance)

13.reason: that these are all the facts settles which ways things could stand do not (Tractatus 2.05; Russell, Logical Atomism V)

14.reason: no list of what is the case, without 'and that's all', settles what is not the case (Russell, Logical Atomism V: general facts cannot be inferred from particular ones)

15.reason: a way things could stand cannot both stand and not stand (Tractatus 2.06 with the law of contradiction)

16.reason: the same exclusion read from the negative side; listed both ways because the word is symmetric

marks.gloss: the shared form of life that words rest on, not itself a claim and neither right nor wrong: what we do and take for granted without saying — that the earth has existed for a long time, that we count this way
marks.source: PI §§19, 241; On Certainty §§94, 105, 204–205; Habermas, the lifeworld

marks.gloss: a word at work in a practice: 'slab!' called on the building site, a greeting, an order, a report
the way to continue that sorts right from wrong: adding 2 after 1000, calling the next red thing 'red'
being able to go on: grasp shown in the next application, not in an inner picture — 'Now I can go on!'
an utterance's offer: it says that something is so, right, or sincerely meant, and binds the speaker to back it — a commitment undertaken
marks.source: Habermas, TCA vol. 1 ch. 3 (validity claims); Brandom, MIE ch. 3 (commitment)

marks.gloss: a hearer's yes or no to a claim, with reasons asked: 'how do you know?', 'why should I?' — the claim put to the test
marks.source: Habermas, TCA vol. 1 ch. 3; Brandom, MIE ch. 4 (default and challenge)

marks.gloss: what was implicit in practice said out as a claim of its own: a rule stated, a definition given, an inference written as an 'if … then'
marks.source: Brandom, MIE ch. 2 and Articulating Reasons, introduction (the expressive role of logical vocabulary)

axioms: Justifications come to an end, and where they end is not a further justification but what we do.
To understand a claim is to know what would make it acceptable; every claim raised can be met with yes or no.
What is made explicit can be challenged; what is background is not challenged while it stays background.
The ground is not true, nor yet false (On Certainty §205).
cast.subject: Meaning in the line of the later Wittgenstein, Habermas and Brandom, without making it norms all the way down: words at work in a shared form of life, the way to go on, understanding, the claim an utterance raises, its challenge, and the rule said out loud, which sinks back into what is taken for granted — read from Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §§2–43, 143–242, and On Certainty §§94–105, 204–205; Habermas, The Theory of Communicative Action (1981) vol. 1 ch. 3 and vol. 2 ch. 6; Brandom, Making It Explicit (1994) chs. 1–4, and Articulating Reasons (2000) introduction

file.concept: Meaning (working name; the corner's name is Arman's to type)
file.cast_by: Virgin Land, 2026-10-09, at Arman's word ('cast our original four concepts in that new shape; drop the logical square; adhere to the concept itself'); poured under MOLD v5 with its amendment §8 of 2026-10-09 (a role is a moment). Every label, word and quality is a proposal until Arman ratifies it.
premises: The Wittgenstein–Habermas–Brandom line is Arman's choice of 2026-09-26 ('drop frege and pick up wittgenstein-habermas-brandom line w/o completely leaning into norms-throughandthrough'). The square of 2026-09-25 (the use, the going-on, the entitlement, the commitment) is dropped at his word of 2026-10-09.
Not norms all the way down: the background is written as neither right nor wrong (a quality on every moment), and the chain of reasons ends in it rather than in a further rule.

Brandom's commitment and entitlement are folded into the claim (a commitment undertaken) and the challenge (entitlement asked for), where his scorekeeping lives; Habermas's validity claims live in the same two moments.

Moments are cut by how meaning shows up and how it moves: the background comes forth as words at work; a practice becomes a way to go on; a way to go on, learned, becomes understanding; one who understands can claim; a claim can be challenged; under challenge the implicit is said out; what is said and accepted sinks back into the background.
open_forks: Does the understanding pass into the claim, or does the claim come straight from the use (a report is a use)? Kept as written: one must be able to go on before one can be held to what one says.
Is the challenge a moment of meaning or of discourse? Kept, with Habermas: to understand a claim is to know what would redeem it under challenge.
The explicit passing into the background: Habermas's lifeworld absorbs what discourse settles; whether every settled claim becomes background, or only some, is left open.
did_not_fit: Sense and reference (Frege): dropped at Arman's word of 2026-09-26.
A private meaning-giving act: refused by the line itself (PI §§243–315); not a moment.

derived_check.ordering: passes into, read as directed: background → use → going-on → understanding → claim → challenge → explicit → background. A closed circle: the one cast of the four whose movement returns to where it began. Marked derived.

passes into.meaning: the first, carried through, becomes the second: the concept's own movement from one moment to the next

presupposes.meaning: the first cannot be what it is unless the second is given

ends in.meaning: pursued as far as it goes, the first comes to rest in the second and goes no further

0.reason: a shared form of life comes forth as words at work: to imagine a language is to imagine a form of life (PI §19)

1.reason: a practice, repeated and taught, becomes a way to go on that sorts right from wrong: following a rule is a custom, a use, an institution (PI §§198–199)

2.reason: a way to go on, learned, becomes an ability: training passes into 'Now I can go on!' (PI §§143–151)

3.reason: one who can go on can say that something is so and be held to it: understanding passes into undertaking commitments (Brandom, MIE ch. 3)

4.reason: a claim, once raised, can be met with a no and a request for reasons (Habermas, TCA vol. 1 ch. 3; Brandom, MIE ch. 4: default and challenge)

5.reason: under challenge, the rule that was implicit in practice is said out as a claim of its own (Brandom, Articulating Reasons, introduction: making it explicit)

6.reason: what is said out and accepted sinks back into what is taken for granted: the river-bed of thoughts shifts, fluid propositions harden into its channel (On Certainty §§96–99; Habermas, TCA vol. 2 ch. 6, the lifeworld)

7.reason: words work only within a form of life: agreement not in opinions but in form of life (PI §§19, 241)

8.reason: a rule exists only in a practice: it is not possible that only one person, once, followed a rule (PI §199)

9.reason: a rule need not be stated to be followed: rules are implicit in practice (PI §201; Brandom, MIE ch. 1)

10.reason: grasping a rule is not an interpretation: one can go on without being able to say the rule (PI §201)

11.reason: only one who understands what she says can be held to it

12.reason: there is nothing to contest without a claim raised

13.reason: the background does not wait to be said, and most of it never is: all testing already takes place within a system (On Certainty §§94, 105)

14.reason: justifications come to an end: asked for reasons, one reaches bedrock — 'this is simply what I do' (PI §217; On Certainty §204)

15.reason: the chain of reasons does not end in a further stated rule: a rule for applying a rule would need another (PI §201, the regress of interpretations)

marks.gloss: the ability to do or not do, both ways at once: the doctor who can heal or harm, the swimmer who can save or stand by
marks.source: Metaphysics Θ.2, 1046b4–7; Θ.5

marks.gloss: what the agent is doing it for, chosen after deliberation, the answer to 'why?': 'to replenish the water supply'
marks.source: NE III.3, 1113a10–11; Anscombe, Intention §§5–6

marks.gloss: the doing in the world: the hand moves, the pump is worked, the word is said — an alteration the agent makes
marks.source: Hegel, Philosophy of Right §115 (the deed); Anscombe, Intention §23

marks.gloss: the not-doing that is done: refraining, keeping silent, letting it happen when one could have done otherwise
marks.source: von Wright, Norm and Action ch. 3

marks.gloss: what follows from the deed or the forbearance in the world, foreseen or not: the house poisoned, the child not saved, the father killed
marks.source: Hegel, Philosophy of Right §118

marks.gloss: the deed as the agent's own: what of it is ascribed to her for praise or blame, and what is not — Oedipus killed his father, but not as a parricide
marks.source: Hegel, Philosophy of Right §117 and its addition; NE III.1

marks.gloss: what repeated deeds make of the agent and what further deeds come from: courage, justice, cowardice — a settled second nature

axioms: Every rational power is a power of contraries: whoever can do can also not do.
Only what was in the purpose is imputed as the agent's action; the rest of what followed is hers only as her deed's consequence.
We become what we repeatedly do, and what we have become shapes what we next choose.
A forbearance is an action only where the deed was in the agent's power.
cast.subject: Action as Aristotle, Hegel and Anscombe take it: a two-way power settled by choice into a deed or a forbearance, the deed running on into outcomes, the agent answering for what was hers, and repeated deeds settling into character that shapes the next choice — read from Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1, III.1–5, VI.12, Metaphysics Θ.2 and Θ.5, De Motu Animalium 7; Hegel, Philosophy of Right §§115–118; Anscombe, Intention (1957) §§5–6, 23; von Wright, Norm and Action (1963) ch. 3

file.concept: Action (working name; the corner's name is Arman's to type)
file.cast_by: Virgin Land, 2026-10-09, at Arman's word ('cast our original four concepts in that new shape; drop the logical square; adhere to the concept itself'); poured under MOLD v5 with its amendment §8 of 2026-10-09 (a role is a moment). Every label, word and quality is a proposal until Arman ratifies it.
premises: The square of 2026-09-25 (the deed, the forbearance, the involuntary doing, the involuntary omission) is dropped at Arman's word of 2026-10-09. The deed and the forbearance are kept as moments, as the two sides of one power; the involuntary is folded into the imputation, as what is not ascribed, since it is the edge where action stops being the agent's.

Moments are cut by the movement Aristotle and Hegel give: a power, deliberating, settles into a purpose; the purpose passes into a deed or a forbearance; these run on into outcomes; outcomes come back to the agent as imputation; repeated deeds become character, and character shapes the next purpose.
Anscombe's 'why?' gives the purpose its determinacy: an action is intentional under the description that answers it.
One quality, 'up to the agent', is declared on every moment (Aristotle's eph' hēmin), because the concept's movement runs from what is up to the agent into what is not.
open_forks: Does a forbearance have outcomes as a deed does? Written holds (the child not saved); causation by omission is disputed.

Negligence: the careless driver is blamed for what he did not purpose, which strains 'the imputation presupposes the purpose'. Hegel's right of knowledge and Aristotle's ignorance through one's own fault (NE III.5, 1113b30–33) pull apart here.
Is the outcome's passing into the imputation a movement of action, or of others' judgment of it? Kept as action's: the agent's own conscience imputes too.
The character is written 'in part' up to the agent: Aristotle's stone, which was up to us to throw and is no longer up to us to recall (NE III.5, 1114a13–21).
did_not_fit: The involuntary (what is done through force or ignorance): the edge of action, not a moment of it; kept as the negative side of the imputation.
Production and action (poiēsis and praxis): a real distinction that cuts across these moments; every moment here has a productive and a practical form.

derived_check.ordering: passes into, read as directed: power → purpose → deed → outcome → imputation; purpose → forbearance → outcome; deed → character → purpose. One cycle (purpose → deed → character → purpose) with a way out of it into the world (outcome, imputation). Refused: outcome ↛ purpose. Marked derived.

passes into.meaning: the first, carried through, becomes the second: the concept's own movement from one moment to the next

presupposes.meaning: the first cannot be what it is unless the second is given

is the other side of.meaning: the first and the second are the two sides of one power: where one is possible, so is the other

0.reason: a two-way power, deliberating, settles on one side: choice is deliberate desire of what is up to us (NE III.3, 1113a10–11)

1.reason: the chosen passes into doing: the conclusion of practical reasoning is an action (De Motu Animalium 7, 701a)

2.reason: the chosen can be a not-doing: refraining on purpose is acting (von Wright, Norm and Action ch. 3)

3.reason: the doing runs on into its consequences in the world, past what was purposed (Hegel, Philosophy of Right §118)

4.reason: what one refrains from leaves the world to run on, and what then happens follows from the refraining: the child not saved (causation by omission is disputed, see open_forks)

5.reason: what followed comes back to the agent as hers or not, in praise and blame (NE III.1, 1109b30–34)

6.reason: what followed cannot become what was purposed after the fact: a purpose is not made by its success or its failure (Hegel, Philosophy of Right §§117–118)

7.reason: repeated deeds become character: we become just by doing just acts (NE II.1, 1103a34–b2)

8.reason: character shapes what is chosen: virtue makes the aim right, practical wisdom the means to it (NE VI.12, 1144a7–9)

9.reason: one deliberates and chooses only about what is up to one and can be done (NE III.3, 1112a30–31)

10.reason: a deed is a power exercised (Metaphysics Θ.5)

11.reason: one can refrain only from what one could do: not doing what one cannot do is no forbearance (von Wright, Norm and Action ch. 3)

12.reason: what is ascribed to the agent as her action is what she knew and purposed: the right of knowledge (Hegel, Philosophy of Right §117); what is done through ignorance of the particulars is not voluntary (NE III.1, 1110b18–1111a21)

13.reason: an attempt that came to nothing is still imputed: the poisoner whose poison failed is a would-be murderer

14.reason: consequences run on whether or not they were purposed (Hegel, Philosophy of Right §118)

15.reason: doing and not doing are the two sides of one rational power (Metaphysics Θ.2, 1046b4–7)

16.reason: the same two sides read from the not-doing; listed both ways because the word is symmetric

marks.gloss: value as what holds rather than what is: binding whether or not anyone wants, knows or does it — truth holding of a theorem, justice holding of a case no court has heard
marks.source: Lotze, Logik §§316–318; Rickert, Der Gegenstand der Erkenntnis

marks.gloss: value's negative pole, which is not its absence: the false, the ugly, the unjust, holding as what ought not to be — an error, a cruelty, a botched work
marks.source: Rickert, value and counter-value (Wert und Unwert)

marks.gloss: value as it faces someone who can fail it: a demand, a norm — 'judge truly', 'keep the promise'; unlike a law of nature it can be broken
marks.source: Windelband, 'Normen und Naturgesetze'; Rickert, the transcendent ought

marks.gloss: a subject's yes or no to an ought: affirming in judgment, approving a deed, honouring a right — or refusing; a real act at a time, by someone
marks.source: Windelband, every judgment contains an appraisal; Rickert, Stellungnahme (taking a position toward a value)

marks.gloss: value as what someone desires or likes: wanting bread, enjoying a song, preferring one coat to another — whether or not anything demands it
marks.source: Lotze (values given in feeling); the psychological value theory of Meinong and Ehrenfels, which the Baden school opposed; Simmel ch. 1 (value and desire)

marks.gloss: a real thing that bears a value: a work, a law, an institution, a theory, a tool well made — value realized in culture
marks.source: Rickert, Kulturwissenschaft und Naturwissenschaft (goods, Güter)

marks.gloss: a reality's mattering for a value, apart from whether anyone approves it: a revolution, a war, a forgery is significant for the values it touches
marks.source: Rickert, value-relation (Wertbeziehung) as distinct from evaluation

marks.gloss: value for the sake of another, relative to need or taste and exchangeable for an equivalent: a market price, a fee, what one would give for it
marks.source: Kant, Groundwork 4:434; Simmel, Philosophie des Geldes ch. 1

axioms: A value holds; it does not exist. Whatever exists — an act, a thing, a price — is real and passes; whatever holds does not pass.
Every value has two poles; the negative pole is not the absence of value but its counter-value.
Where an ought holds, failing it is possible; where failing is impossible there is a law of nature, not an ought.
Whatever has a price can be replaced by an equivalent; what holds has none.
cast.subject: Value as the Neo-Kantians take it, Kant behind them and Simmel beside them: what holds rather than what is, how it faces a subject who can fail it, how it is answered with a yes or a no, borne by real goods, made significant in history, and priced in exchange — read from Lotze, Logik (1874) §§316–318; Windelband, 'Normen und Naturgesetze' (1882, in Präludien); Rickert, Der Gegenstand der Erkenntnis (1892/1904) and Kulturwissenschaft und Naturwissenschaft (1899); Kant, Groundwork 4:434; Simmel, Philosophie des Geldes (1900) ch. 1

file.concept: Value (working name; the corner's name is Arman's to type)
file.cast_by: Virgin Land, 2026-10-09, at Arman's word ('cast our original four concepts in that new shape; drop the logical square; adhere to the concept itself'); poured under MOLD v5 with its amendment §8 of 2026-10-09 (a role is a moment). Every label, word and quality is a proposal until Arman ratifies it.
premises: The Neo-Kantian backbone is Arman's choice of 2026-09-25 ('for value, use neo-kantians'). The logical square of that day (self-value, self-disvalue, conditional value, conditional disvalue) is dropped at his word of 2026-10-09.

Moments are cut by how value shows up and how it moves: it holds; facing a subject it becomes an ought; the subject answers it; the answer, carried into work, becomes a good; the good, once real, matters in history; offered in exchange, it takes a price.

The acknowledging and the wanting are kept as two moments: answering an ought and desiring a thing are two ways value shows up, and the Neo-Kantians' case against psychologism rests on keeping them apart.

Polarity (true and false, beautiful and ugly, just and unjust) is kept as one moment, the counter-value, opposed to the validity, rather than as an axis crossing every moment; it is the negative pole, not the absence of value.
Kant and Simmel are admitted for the price because the Neo-Kantians' own contrast of what holds with what is merely wanted or exchanged needs that moment on the page.
The value-free, mere nature, is left out as the concept's edge; Rickert's third realm of meaning is left out (did_not_fit).
open_forks: Is the significance real? It sits on real things but is a relation to a value; 'exists in time' is written UNKNOWN.
Does the counter-value hold in the same sense as the value? Rickert pairs them; whether 'the false holds' as truth holds is left open.
Does the ought exist in time? Rickert's transcendent ought does not; a promise made today creates an ought that did not exist yesterday. Written 'no', with Rickert.
did_not_fit: Rickert's third realm, meaning (Sinn), the immanent sense of the valuing act (System der Philosophie, 1921): a moment of value in his late system, left out so that Value is not cast toward Meaning.
The ranking of values (higher and lower; Rickert's six domains, 'Vom System der Werte', 1913): an ordering among values, not a moment of value; the mold forbids handing in a ranking.
The value-free, nature as mere reality: the concept's edge.

derived_check.ordering: passes into, read as directed: validity → ought → acknowledging → good → significance; good → price; wanting → price. Refused: validity ↛ price, price ↛ validity, significance ↛ validity. Two roots, what holds and what is wanted, meeting only in the good's price; no movement returns to the validity. Marked derived.

passes into.meaning: the first, carried through, becomes the second: the concept's own movement from one moment to the next

presupposes.meaning: the first cannot be what it is unless the second is given

is borne by.meaning: the first is present in the second as in its bearer

opposes.meaning: the first and the second are the two poles of one value, each excluding the other

0.reason: a value that holds, faced by a subject who can fall short of it, becomes a demand: truth turns into the ought of judging truly (Rickert, the transcendent ought; Windelband, 'Normen und Naturgesetze')

1.reason: a demand is met by a yes or a no: to judge is to affirm what ought to be affirmed (Windelband; Rickert, Der Gegenstand der Erkenntnis)

2.reason: a value affirmed and carried into work becomes a good: the affirmed truth a theory, the honoured right a law (Rickert, Kulturwissenschaft und Naturwissenschaft)

3.reason: a good, once real, comes to matter beyond its makers' approval: it becomes significant for whoever relates it to its value (Rickert, value-relation)

4.reason: a good offered in exchange takes on a price: its value becomes what another would give for it (Simmel, Philosophie des Geldes ch. 1)

5.reason: what holds has no equivalent: it is raised above all price (Kant, Groundwork 4:434)

6.reason: no price, however high, makes a thing hold: whatever has a price can be replaced by an equivalent (Kant, Groundwork 4:434)

7.reason: no amount of mattering in history makes a value hold: validity is not made by significance (Windelband's and Rickert's case against historicism)

8.reason: there is no ought without a value that holds: a norm is a value turned toward a subject (Windelband)

9.reason: an ought addresses only one who could fail it; where failing were impossible there would be a law of nature, not a norm (Windelband, 'Normen und Naturgesetze')

10.reason: a truth holds whether or not anyone affirms it (Lotze, Logik §316; Rickert against psychologism)

11.reason: a price exists only where someone wants: market price is relative to need, fancy price to taste (Kant, Groundwork 4:434)

12.reason: a reality matters only relative to a value that holds (Rickert: value-relation presupposes values)

13.reason: a thing can matter for a value without anyone approving it: the historian relates a war to political values without praising it (Rickert, Kulturwissenschaft und Naturwissenschaft: value-relation is not evaluation)

14.reason: a value that holds is present in a good as in its bearer: justice in a law, truth in a theory (Rickert: goods are realities to which values attach)

15.reason: a value is not in the act that affirms it: the act is real and passes, the value holds (Rickert against psychologism)

16.reason: a price sits on a thing offered in exchange (Simmel ch. 1)

17.reason: true and false, beautiful and ugly, just and unjust: the two poles of one value, each excluding the other (Rickert, Wert und Unwert)

18.reason: the same opposition read from the negative pole; listed both ways because the word is symmetric

19.reason: what holds does not hold because it is wanted: value is not desirability (the Baden school against the psychological value theory of Meinong and Ehrenfels)

20.reason: a yes or no is an acknowledging only as the answer to a demand; a mere liking is wanting, not acknowledging (Rickert)

21.reason: one can want what no ought demands, and want what an ought forbids

22.reason: a want that meets a thing another holds becomes an offer: desire, through exchange, sets a price (Simmel, Philosophie des Geldes ch. 1)

marks.gloss: a way things could stand, before or apart from whether it does: the cat's being on the mat, the train's arriving at nine
marks.source: Tractatus 2.012–2.0141 (states of affairs and their possibility)

marks.gloss: a way things stand: what is the case, here and now — the cat is on the mat
marks.source: Tractatus 2: what is the case, a fact, is the existence of states of affairs

marks.gloss: a way things could stand that does not, which is itself the case: there is no cat on the mat; the train did not come
marks.source: Tractatus 2.06; Russell, Logical Atomism III (negative facts)

marks.gloss: that these are all the facts and nothing besides: the world as everything that is the case — 'and that's all'
marks.source: Tractatus 1.1–1.12; Russell, Logical Atomism V (general facts)

marks.gloss: what has been the case and can no longer be otherwise: the battle was fought, the word was said
marks.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.2, 1139b7–11 (citing Agathon)

marks.gloss: a fact ascertained and held so that it can be cited: the facts of the case, a measured value, a date fixed by documents
marks.source: Fleck, Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact; Austin, 'Truth'

marks.gloss: a fact that is the case because it is counted as the case: a debt, a marriage, a border, a goal scored
marks.source: Searle, Construction of Social Reality ch. 2 ('X counts as Y in C'); Anscombe, 'On Brute Facts'

axioms: Every fact is a way things could stand that stands; every negative fact a way things could stand that does not.
What has been the case cannot be made not to have been.
No set of positive facts settles the negative ones without the fact that they are all.
An established fact can be revised; a done fact cannot.
A fact that is the case because it is counted stops being the case when the counting stops.
cast.subject: Fact: what is the case, read as the concept moves — from a way things could stand, to its standing or not standing, to its having been and being settled, to its being ascertained and held, with the totality that settles what is not, and facts that are the case because they are counted — read from Wittgenstein, Tractatus 1–2.06; Russell, The Philosophy of Logical Atomism (1918) lectures III and V; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.2; Austin, 'Truth' (1950); Anscombe, 'On Brute Facts' (1958); Searle, The Construction of Social Reality (1995) ch. 2; Fleck, Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact (1935)

file.concept: Fact (working name; the corner's name is Arman's to type)
file.cast_by: Virgin Land, 2026-10-09, at Arman's word ('cast our original four concepts in that new shape; drop the logical square; adhere to the concept itself'); poured under MOLD v5 with its amendment §8 of 2026-10-09 (a role is a moment). Every label, word and quality is a proposal until Arman ratifies it.
premises: The logical square of 2026-09-25 (general and particular, positive and negative facts) is dropped at Arman's word of 2026-10-09. Two of its insights survive as moments: the not-obtaining (Russell's negative fact) and the totality (Russell's general fact, Wittgenstein's 'all the facts').

Moments are cut by how fact shows up and how it moves: a way things could stand comes to stand or fails to; what stands passes and becomes what has been, which can no longer be otherwise; what has been is ascertained and held; some facts are the case only because they are counted as the case.

Brute facts are the default here; the instituted is the moment where being counted makes a fact the case (Searle), resting on facts that are the case without being counted (Anscombe: bruteness is relative).
The fact as a true thought (Frege) and as what a true statement states (Strawson) are theories of where facts live, not moments of fact (did_not_fit).
open_forks: Does the established pass into the instituted? Fleck and those after him would say a scientific fact is made by its collective; written does-not-hold, with that fork open.
Is the totality a fact among facts (Russell's general fact) or the frame of all facts (Tractatus 1.11)? Kept as one moment.
Are there negative facts, or only the non-existence of positive ones? Kept as a moment because the concept, as used, has them: 'the train did not come' is a fact one reports.
The done: does it pass into the established always, or only when someone takes it up? Most of what has been is never ascertained; the movement is written as the concept's, not as what always happens.
did_not_fit: The fact as a true thought (Frege, 'Der Gedanke', 1918) and as what a true statement states (Strawson, 'Truth', 1950): theories of where facts live, not moments of fact.
The value-laden fact (thick concepts; the entanglement of fact and value): the meeting of Fact with Value is the edge's business, not this cast's.

derived_check.ordering: passes into, read as directed: possible → obtaining → done → established; possible → not-obtaining. Refused: done ↛ obtaining, established ↛ instituted. A line with one branch and no return: the concept runs one way, from could-be to settled and held. Marked derived.

passes into.meaning: the first, carried through, becomes the second: the concept's own movement from one moment to the next

presupposes.meaning: the first cannot be what it is unless the second is given

settles.meaning: the first fixes which instances of the second there are

excludes.meaning: the first and the second cannot both hold of the same way things could stand

0.reason: a way things could stand comes to stand: the coin lands heads (Tractatus 2)

1.reason: a way things could stand fails to stand, and its failing is itself a fact (Tractatus 2.06; Russell, Logical Atomism III)

2.reason: what is the case passes and becomes what has been the case

3.reason: what has been cannot come to be the case again as the same fact; a repetition is another fact (Aristotle, NE VI.2: not even a god can make undone what has been done)

4.reason: what has been the case is taken up, ascertained and recorded, and becomes a fact one can cite (Fleck)

5.reason: ascertaining finds a fact, it does not make one: a fact recorded does not become a fact that is the case by being counted (Searle's line between brute and institutional facts; Fleck would contest it, see open_forks)

6.reason: what is the case is one of the ways things could stand (Tractatus 2.012–2.0141)

7.reason: only what could be the case can fail to be the case: there is no negative fact of the impossible

8.reason: a way things could stand needs nothing to be the case to be possible

9.reason: only what is or was the case can be established; a record of what is not the case is an error, not an established fact

10.reason: what is the case does not wait to be ascertained: the fact comes before its record (Austin, 'Truth': statements correspond to facts, they do not make them)

11.reason: a fact that is the case by being counted needs something that is the case to be counted as it: the paper for money, the words said for a marriage (Searle ch. 2; Anscombe: bruteness is relative)

12.reason: a debt, a border, a price is the case only while it is held as the case and can be cited (Searle: collective acceptance)

13.reason: that these are all the facts settles which ways things could stand do not (Tractatus 2.05; Russell, Logical Atomism V)

14.reason: no list of what is the case, without 'and that's all', settles what is not the case (Russell, Logical Atomism V: general facts cannot be inferred from particular ones)

15.reason: a way things could stand cannot both stand and not stand (Tractatus 2.06 with the law of contradiction)

16.reason: the same exclusion read from the negative side; listed both ways because the word is symmetric

marks.gloss: the shared form of life that words rest on, not itself a claim and neither right nor wrong: what we do and take for granted without saying — that the earth has existed for a long time, that we count this way
marks.source: PI §§19, 241; On Certainty §§94, 105, 204–205; Habermas, the lifeworld

marks.gloss: a word at work in a practice: 'slab!' called on the building site, a greeting, an order, a report
the way to continue that sorts right from wrong: adding 2 after 1000, calling the next red thing 'red'
being able to go on: grasp shown in the next application, not in an inner picture — 'Now I can go on!'
an utterance's offer: it says that something is so, right, or sincerely meant, and binds the speaker to back it — a commitment undertaken
marks.source: Habermas, TCA vol. 1 ch. 3 (validity claims); Brandom, MIE ch. 3 (commitment)

marks.gloss: a hearer's yes or no to a claim, with reasons asked: 'how do you know?', 'why should I?' — the claim put to the test
marks.source: Habermas, TCA vol. 1 ch. 3; Brandom, MIE ch. 4 (default and challenge)

marks.gloss: what was implicit in practice said out as a claim of its own: a rule stated, a definition given, an inference written as an 'if … then'
marks.source: Brandom, MIE ch. 2 and Articulating Reasons, introduction (the expressive role of logical vocabulary)

axioms: Justifications come to an end, and where they end is not a further justification but what we do.
To understand a claim is to know what would make it acceptable; every claim raised can be met with yes or no.
What is made explicit can be challenged; what is background is not challenged while it stays background.
The ground is not true, nor yet false (On Certainty §205).
cast.subject: Meaning in the line of the later Wittgenstein, Habermas and Brandom, without making it norms all the way down: words at work in a shared form of life, the way to go on, understanding, the claim an utterance raises, its challenge, and the rule said out loud, which sinks back into what is taken for granted — read from Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §§2–43, 143–242, and On Certainty §§94–105, 204–205; Habermas, The Theory of Communicative Action (1981) vol. 1 ch. 3 and vol. 2 ch. 6; Brandom, Making It Explicit (1994) chs. 1–4, and Articulating Reasons (2000) introduction

file.concept: Meaning (working name; the corner's name is Arman's to type)
file.cast_by: Virgin Land, 2026-10-09, at Arman's word ('cast our original four concepts in that new shape; drop the logical square; adhere to the concept itself'); poured under MOLD v5 with its amendment §8 of 2026-10-09 (a role is a moment). Every label, word and quality is a proposal until Arman ratifies it.
premises: The Wittgenstein–Habermas–Brandom line is Arman's choice of 2026-09-26 ('drop frege and pick up wittgenstein-habermas-brandom line w/o completely leaning into norms-throughandthrough'). The square of 2026-09-25 (the use, the going-on, the entitlement, the commitment) is dropped at his word of 2026-10-09.
Not norms all the way down: the background is written as neither right nor wrong (a quality on every moment), and the chain of reasons ends in it rather than in a further rule.

Brandom's commitment and entitlement are folded into the claim (a commitment undertaken) and the challenge (entitlement asked for), where his scorekeeping lives; Habermas's validity claims live in the same two moments.

Moments are cut by how meaning shows up and how it moves: the background comes forth as words at work; a practice becomes a way to go on; a way to go on, learned, becomes understanding; one who understands can claim; a claim can be challenged; under challenge the implicit is said out; what is said and accepted sinks back into the background.
open_forks: Does the understanding pass into the claim, or does the claim come straight from the use (a report is a use)? Kept as written: one must be able to go on before one can be held to what one says.
Is the challenge a moment of meaning or of discourse? Kept, with Habermas: to understand a claim is to know what would redeem it under challenge.
The explicit passing into the background: Habermas's lifeworld absorbs what discourse settles; whether every settled claim becomes background, or only some, is left open.
did_not_fit: Sense and reference (Frege): dropped at Arman's word of 2026-09-26.
A private meaning-giving act: refused by the line itself (PI §§243–315); not a moment.

derived_check.ordering: passes into, read as directed: background → use → going-on → understanding → claim → challenge → explicit → background. A closed circle: the one cast of the four whose movement returns to where it began. Marked derived.

passes into.meaning: the first, carried through, becomes the second: the concept's own movement from one moment to the next

presupposes.meaning: the first cannot be what it is unless the second is given

ends in.meaning: pursued as far as it goes, the first comes to rest in the second and goes no further

0.reason: a shared form of life comes forth as words at work: to imagine a language is to imagine a form of life (PI §19)

1.reason: a practice, repeated and taught, becomes a way to go on that sorts right from wrong: following a rule is a custom, a use, an institution (PI §§198–199)

2.reason: a way to go on, learned, becomes an ability: training passes into 'Now I can go on!' (PI §§143–151)

3.reason: one who can go on can say that something is so and be held to it: understanding passes into undertaking commitments (Brandom, MIE ch. 3)

4.reason: a claim, once raised, can be met with a no and a request for reasons (Habermas, TCA vol. 1 ch. 3; Brandom, MIE ch. 4: default and challenge)

5.reason: under challenge, the rule that was implicit in practice is said out as a claim of its own (Brandom, Articulating Reasons, introduction: making it explicit)

6.reason: what is said out and accepted sinks back into what is taken for granted: the river-bed of thoughts shifts, fluid propositions harden into its channel (On Certainty §§96–99; Habermas, TCA vol. 2 ch. 6, the lifeworld)

7.reason: words work only within a form of life: agreement not in opinions but in form of life (PI §§19, 241)

8.reason: a rule exists only in a practice: it is not possible that only one person, once, followed a rule (PI §199)

9.reason: a rule need not be stated to be followed: rules are implicit in practice (PI §201; Brandom, MIE ch. 1)

10.reason: grasping a rule is not an interpretation: one can go on without being able to say the rule (PI §201)

11.reason: only one who understands what she says can be held to it

12.reason: there is nothing to contest without a claim raised

13.reason: the background does not wait to be said, and most of it never is: all testing already takes place within a system (On Certainty §§94, 105)

14.reason: justifications come to an end: asked for reasons, one reaches bedrock — 'this is simply what I do' (PI §217; On Certainty §204)

15.reason: the chain of reasons does not end in a further stated rule: a rule for applying a rule would need another (PI §201, the regress of interpretations)

marks.gloss: the ability to do or not do, both ways at once: the doctor who can heal or harm, the swimmer who can save or stand by
marks.source: Metaphysics Θ.2, 1046b4–7; Θ.5

marks.gloss: what the agent is doing it for, chosen after deliberation, the answer to 'why?': 'to replenish the water supply'
marks.source: NE III.3, 1113a10–11; Anscombe, Intention §§5–6

marks.gloss: the doing in the world: the hand moves, the pump is worked, the word is said — an alteration the agent makes
marks.source: Hegel, Philosophy of Right §115 (the deed); Anscombe, Intention §23

marks.gloss: the not-doing that is done: refraining, keeping silent, letting it happen when one could have done otherwise
marks.source: von Wright, Norm and Action ch. 3

marks.gloss: what follows from the deed or the forbearance in the world, foreseen or not: the house poisoned, the child not saved, the father killed
marks.source: Hegel, Philosophy of Right §118

marks.gloss: the deed as the agent's own: what of it is ascribed to her for praise or blame, and what is not — Oedipus killed his father, but not as a parricide
marks.source: Hegel, Philosophy of Right §117 and its addition; NE III.1

marks.gloss: what repeated deeds make of the agent and what further deeds come from: courage, justice, cowardice — a settled second nature

axioms: Every rational power is a power of contraries: whoever can do can also not do.
Only what was in the purpose is imputed as the agent's action; the rest of what followed is hers only as her deed's consequence.
We become what we repeatedly do, and what we have become shapes what we next choose.
A forbearance is an action only where the deed was in the agent's power.
cast.subject: Action as Aristotle, Hegel and Anscombe take it: a two-way power settled by choice into a deed or a forbearance, the deed running on into outcomes, the agent answering for what was hers, and repeated deeds settling into character that shapes the next choice — read from Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1, III.1–5, VI.12, Metaphysics Θ.2 and Θ.5, De Motu Animalium 7; Hegel, Philosophy of Right §§115–118; Anscombe, Intention (1957) §§5–6, 23; von Wright, Norm and Action (1963) ch. 3

file.concept: Action (working name; the corner's name is Arman's to type)
file.cast_by: Virgin Land, 2026-10-09, at Arman's word ('cast our original four concepts in that new shape; drop the logical square; adhere to the concept itself'); poured under MOLD v5 with its amendment §8 of 2026-10-09 (a role is a moment). Every label, word and quality is a proposal until Arman ratifies it.
premises: The square of 2026-09-25 (the deed, the forbearance, the involuntary doing, the involuntary omission) is dropped at Arman's word of 2026-10-09. The deed and the forbearance are kept as moments, as the two sides of one power; the involuntary is folded into the imputation, as what is not ascribed, since it is the edge where action stops being the agent's.

Moments are cut by the movement Aristotle and Hegel give: a power, deliberating, settles into a purpose; the purpose passes into a deed or a forbearance; these run on into outcomes; outcomes come back to the agent as imputation; repeated deeds become character, and character shapes the next purpose.
Anscombe's 'why?' gives the purpose its determinacy: an action is intentional under the description that answers it.
One quality, 'up to the agent', is declared on every moment (Aristotle's eph' hēmin), because the concept's movement runs from what is up to the agent into what is not.
open_forks: Does a forbearance have outcomes as a deed does? Written holds (the child not saved); causation by omission is disputed.

Negligence: the careless driver is blamed for what he did not purpose, which strains 'the imputation presupposes the purpose'. Hegel's right of knowledge and Aristotle's ignorance through one's own fault (NE III.5, 1113b30–33) pull apart here.
Is the outcome's passing into the imputation a movement of action, or of others' judgment of it? Kept as action's: the agent's own conscience imputes too.
The character is written 'in part' up to the agent: Aristotle's stone, which was up to us to throw and is no longer up to us to recall (NE III.5, 1114a13–21).
did_not_fit: The involuntary (what is done through force or ignorance): the edge of action, not a moment of it; kept as the negative side of the imputation.
Production and action (poiēsis and praxis): a real distinction that cuts across these moments; every moment here has a productive and a practical form.

derived_check.ordering: passes into, read as directed: power → purpose → deed → outcome → imputation; purpose → forbearance → outcome; deed → character → purpose. One cycle (purpose → deed → character → purpose) with a way out of it into the world (outcome, imputation). Refused: outcome ↛ purpose. Marked derived.

passes into.meaning: the first, carried through, becomes the second: the concept's own movement from one moment to the next

presupposes.meaning: the first cannot be what it is unless the second is given

is the other side of.meaning: the first and the second are the two sides of one power: where one is possible, so is the other

0.reason: a two-way power, deliberating, settles on one side: choice is deliberate desire of what is up to us (NE III.3, 1113a10–11)

1.reason: the chosen passes into doing: the conclusion of practical reasoning is an action (De Motu Animalium 7, 701a)

2.reason: the chosen can be a not-doing: refraining on purpose is acting (von Wright, Norm and Action ch. 3)

3.reason: the doing runs on into its consequences in the world, past what was purposed (Hegel, Philosophy of Right §118)

4.reason: what one refrains from leaves the world to run on, and what then happens follows from the refraining: the child not saved (causation by omission is disputed, see open_forks)

5.reason: what followed comes back to the agent as hers or not, in praise and blame (NE III.1, 1109b30–34)

6.reason: what followed cannot become what was purposed after the fact: a purpose is not made by its success or its failure (Hegel, Philosophy of Right §§117–118)

7.reason: repeated deeds become character: we become just by doing just acts (NE II.1, 1103a34–b2)

8.reason: character shapes what is chosen: virtue makes the aim right, practical wisdom the means to it (NE VI.12, 1144a7–9)

9.reason: one deliberates and chooses only about what is up to one and can be done (NE III.3, 1112a30–31)

10.reason: a deed is a power exercised (Metaphysics Θ.5)

11.reason: one can refrain only from what one could do: not doing what one cannot do is no forbearance (von Wright, Norm and Action ch. 3)

12.reason: what is ascribed to the agent as her action is what she knew and purposed: the right of knowledge (Hegel, Philosophy of Right §117); what is done through ignorance of the particulars is not voluntary (NE III.1, 1110b18–1111a21)

13.reason: an attempt that came to nothing is still imputed: the poisoner whose poison failed is a would-be murderer

14.reason: consequences run on whether or not they were purposed (Hegel, Philosophy of Right §118)

15.reason: doing and not doing are the two sides of one rational power (Metaphysics Θ.2, 1046b4–7)

16.reason: the same two sides read from the not-doing; listed both ways because the word is symmetric

2: the ground is not true, nor yet false (OC 205): the background does not hold as a value holds; it is what we do
the background is not a yes or a no: it comes before every taking of position
among values the background is the lived ethos: a culture's goods taken for granted, its works, customs, institutions (a little forced: the good is one thing, the background a whole)

the background is the world-picture against which true and false are told apart (OC 94): among facts, the totality as frame (a little forced: the totality is all the facts, the background the frame they are told against)
the background is not established by grounds: all testing takes place within it (OC 105, 204)
agreement in form of life, not in opinions (PI 241): the background is not the case because anyone counts it so
a rule exists only in a practice (PI 199); a validity holds whether or not anyone follows it (Lotze): Meaning refuses that picture of a rule
the way to go on sorts right from wrong and can be failed: it faces the learner as a demand
following a rule is a custom, a use, an institution (PI 199): the right way to go on is the case because it is how we count it
to understand a claim is to know what would make it acceptable, not to accept it (Habermas): one can understand and say no
to understand a sentence is to know what would be the case if it were true, whether or not it is (Tractatus 4.024) (a little forced: an ability, grasping a possible state)
one understands a false sentence as well as a true one: understanding does not need what is said to be the case
to assert is to affirm, a yes given to what ought to be affirmed (Windelband, Rickert); to claim is to undertake a commitment (Brandom)
a claim puts forward a way things could stand as standing: its content is a possible state, and whether it stands is what a challenge tests
a claim is not yet a fact on record: it waits to be redeemed under challenge (Habermas)
the hearer's yes or no to a claim is a taking of position (Habermas's yes/no; Rickert's Stellungnahme)
said out, a rule faces those who follow it as a demand that can be failed and contested
a rule said out and adopted is the case because it is counted as the case: a definition, a codified law

1: a power is a possibility in the agent, had when not exercised (Metaphysics Theta 3, against the Megarians): what she can do is a way things could stand
one chooses what one has judged best: the purpose is a yes given to an end (NE III.2-3)
choice is deliberate desire (NE III.3, 1113a10): in value, the purpose is a wanting
what is purposed is a way things could stand that does not yet: the state to be brought about
no one deliberates about what is already the case (NE III.3; VI.2): what is purposed is not yet
a deed is a real thing that bears a value, as a work does: the just act (a little forced: a deed bears the counter-value as readily)
a deed, as fact, is a thing done, factum, which not even a god can undo (Agathon in NE VI.2)
a forbearance, as fact, is a negative fact: he did not speak, she did not pull the lever
what follows matters for the values it touches, approved or not: the unintended consequence is history's material (Hegel PR 118; Rickert)
what follows is what comes to be the case
to impute is to judge someone the author of a deed under a law (Kant, Metaphysics of Morals 6:227): a yes or no given to the deed as hers
an imputation is not a finding of fact: it can be defeated by excuses without any fact being denied (Hart 1949)
'he did it' ascribes responsibility rather than describes: an ascription is the case because it is counted (Hart, 'The Ascription of Responsibility and Rights', 1949)
a virtue is a praiseworthy state, a good of the person (NE I.13) (a little forced: a vice bears the counter-value)
a character is deeds settled into what one is; like the stone thrown, it cannot be recalled (NE III.5) (a little forced: the done is past, a character present)
